title: Om mani padme hum
hookLine: six syllables, spun in prayer wheels and carved into stones along mountain paths

cards: A brass cylinder the size of a coffee can, set on a handle. An older woman walks around a temple, turning it with a flick of the wrist, clockwise, again and again, her lips moving.
Along the path outside, flat stones are stacked into walls, each carved with the same row of letters. Up on the ridge, prayer flags carry them too.
Inside the cylinder, tightly rolled, is paper printed over and over with those letters. The whole landscape seems to be saying one sentence: six syllables that Tibetan Buddhists tie to compassion.

teach.b: Om mani padme hum is a mantra, a sacred sound to be repeated, the kind of word you met back on day one hundred two. First, whose sound it is.

Tibetan Buddhists connect it with Avalokiteshvara, called Chenrezig in Tibetan, the bodhisattva of compassion, the one who hears the cries of the world. A Mahayana scripture, the Karandavyuha Sutra, praises it at length.
To say it is to turn the mind toward that compassion. Second, the words.

teach.h: JEWEL, LOTUS, AND A GRAMMAR DEBATE.
teach.b: Mani is a jewel; padma is a lotus. So a common English rendering is your line: the jewel in the lotus. That's a start, not a settled one.

Scholars argue over the grammar, and Tibetan teachers often skip the translation and explain the syllables one at a time, each linked to a quality to cultivate or a kind of suffering to be freed from.
Third, the wheel and the stone. Written inside a prayer wheel, the mantra is said to be sent out with every turn.
Carved on a stone, it stays there for every passerby. Printed on a flag, the wind carries it. Compassion shouldn't depend on one person remembering to say it.
The lotus grows up out of mud and opens clean, an image teachers use for a mind that stays open in a messy world. The jewel is something precious that was there all along.
You don't need to settle the grammar to hold both pictures.

how: Tibetan Buddhists often recite om mani padme hum on prayer beads, turn prayer wheels that contain it, and carve or print it on stones and flags, as an expression of the compassion of Chenrezig.

games.q: what does “om mani padme hum” mean?
o: the Tibetan mantra of compassion, linked to Chenrezig
the Buddha's last words, spoken to his followers
a Tibetan greeting that means peace be with you

games.q: om mani padme hum: tap the pairs.

s: the jewel in the lotus is the one settled translation
it's a common rendering. scholars argue over the grammar, and teachers often explain the syllables one by one instead.
the mantra is written inside prayer wheels and carved on stones
it's spun, carved and printed on flags, so it's sent out without anyone having to remember to say it.
Tibetan Buddhists connect the mantra with Chenrezig
Avalokiteshvara in Sanskrit, the bodhisattva of compassion.

games.q: you're walking a path in a Tibetan valley and pass a wall of stones, each carved with the mantra. what are the stones there to do?
o: mark the boundary of a monastery's land.
keep the mantra present for every passerby.
record the names of people buried nearby.
games.why: carved on a stone, the mantra stays there for everyone who walks by. compassion that doesn't depend on someone remembering to say it.

practice: If you'd like, say the mantra softly, om mani padme hum, at an easy, steady pace, the way it's said in Tibetan homes and temples.

If saying it doesn't fit you, listen to it inwardly, or rest with the breath and the picture of a lotus opening above muddy water. There's nothing to achieve; let the sound, or the quiet, do the work.

wordCard.voice: Om mani padme hum. The mantra of compassion in Tibetan Buddhism, linked to Chenrezig, spun in wheels and carved in stone. Often rendered the jewel in the lotus. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari. Tibetans often say it om mani peme hung.

carryVoice: Your line: the jewel in the lotus. Something precious, open in the mud. Until tomorrow.
